episodes.title: Chamath: Bitcoin Goes to Zero, Robots vs. $40T Debt, Elon’s SpaceX Shares for 72M Kids | EP #304
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis hosts a Moonshots crossover with the original crew (Alex Wissner-Gross, Dave Blundin, and Salim Ismail) and All-In co-host Chamath Palihapitiya. The episode opens on Anthropic's new Public Benefit Fund: 5% of shares committed now, with up to 2% more at the board's discretion for every 50% rise in value, which Peter pegs at roughly $75 to $100 billion ahead of an IPO. Chamath says the founders are sincere but questions what fail-safe exists if the fund mean-reverts like most big philanthropies, and calls the Giving Pledge reputation washing. Alex reads Anthropic's choice of a private fund as a snub to universal basic equity, Salim calls philanthropy a scarcity-era response, and Dave notes how hard the dilution vote will make the board's job.

The second story is Elon Musk's pledge to give one SpaceX share to each of the 72 million American kids, about $10.5 billion or $146 per child through Trump accounts. Chamath calls it the better version of the Giving Pledge, Dave argues future value comes from asset ownership rather than paychecks, and Alex sees both universal basic equity and clever marketing for a possible Tesla-SpaceX merger.

Clips from Walter Isaacson's interview with Elon drive the middle of the show. On a post-money economy measured in wattage and tonnage, Chamath explains his roughly 6 gigawatt power position: US electricity demand outruns supply even if every planned project is built, small reactors face the same permitting burden as large ones, and solar was the fastest path, which led him into data centers. He argues AGI already exists but cannot diffuse because of build-out constraints such as utility co-ops, skilled-labor shortages, and hyperscalers withholding compute, and predicts a massive compute shortage in the next three or four years. Alex counters that demand and model distillation matter too.

On Elon's doubt that humans stay in control of superintelligence, Chamath wants labs' founding documents to be inspectable, Dave says inspection matters more than training now that self-improving open models exist, and Alex argues for competition, defensive co-scaling, and merging with machines. On the $40 trillion national debt, Chamath says AI, robots, and new drugs like GLP-1s won't erase the debt so much as make it less important, while Alex imagines automation quietly rebasing defense and entitlement spending.

The panel also covers Bill Gross's free idealab.ai platform with more than 1.2 billion AI-generated business ideas, which Chamath says matters less than execution, and the alleged OpenAI conference-room bugging case. In a closing hot seat, Chamath says Bitcoin is capped and will eventually be hacked to zero, backs a ranked free-cash-flow approach over the S&P 500, explains why he now avoids chip startups for power and data centers, and says he is the least invested he has been in 15 years.

episodes.title: Flying Tesla Car, Robot Brains Halving in Cost Every 3 Weeks, and Why Incentives Decide AI Alignment
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis records this Moonshots episode in the podcast studio with Salim Ismail and Emad Mostaque, plus special guest Anousheh Ansari, CEO of XPRIZE, just after XPRIZE's annual Visioneering event. Peter retells how he found Anousheh in 2001 while struggling to fund the original $10 million spaceflight competition, which was renamed the Ansari XPRIZE in her family's honor; she later flew to the space station on a Soyuz and became the first private female astronaut.

The news segment opens with Tesla's flying Roadster demo in Waco, Texas, next to SpaceX's McGregor test site. The car drove upside down along a curved ramp using a fan suction system that can pull up to 2 Gs, then hopped using compressed-air thrusters built with SpaceX technology. Peter cites 0 to 60 in under a second, a 230 mph top speed, and production starting in 2028 per Elon and the group asks who could regulate or insure it. Next, Emad walks through RoboCurve's Robo Dojo benchmark, where the cost for a frontier model to complete a robot subtask fell from $2.36 in July to 38 cents in September, an 84% drop that amounts to halving every three weeks. The mates argue generalist models are beating specialist ones, debate whether robots start in dull, dirty, dangerous work or in surgery, and question whether the humanoid is the right form factor. The third story is a test of 50 unpublished research-level physics problems that GPT-6 Astra answered for about $3 each; it was first scored 49 of 50 until the published answer to the last problem turned out to be wrong.

The middle of the episode is about incentives. Peter names fear, greed, curiosity, and love as human drivers and recounts historical prizes: the 1714 Longitude Prize won by clockmaker John Harrison, the French food-preservation prize that produced canning, and the $25,000 prize behind Lindbergh's flight. Anousheh says every dollar of XPRIZE purse has driven about 62 times its value in economic impact, with teams raising roughly $12 billion in investment. They cover the oil spill cleanup prize, where a dentist and a tattoo artist took second place, a new $5 million Habitable Worlds prize that uses AI on telescope data, an accelerated-learning prize for first graders in India and Africa, and the Visioneering-winning organ biostasis prize, which aims to keep organs viable for six months.

The last stretch turns to AI alignment and human purpose. Peter flags the race with China, engagement business models, reward hacking, and evaluation gaming as misaligning incentives, and floats insurance-backed standards like Underwriters Laboratories plus alignment prizes. Salim notes humans don't share one set of values to begin with, while Emad argues models grow like sprawling cities and that the training data and curriculum a model starts with matter most. The closing discussion argues that as AI and robots do more of the doing, people can spend more time being and find meaning through community and shared purpose, and Peter ends by distinguishing a passion from a purpose.

episodes.title: OpenAI Bulk-Solves 722 Math Problems, Anthropic’s Cruelty Policy, & Elon’s Quadrillion-Dollar SpaceX
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis hosts this Moonshots episode, released October 15, with Alex Wissner-Gross, Dave Blundin, and Salim Ismail (live from Singapore). Peter opens on two headline numbers: OpenAI publishing 722 math solutions on GitHub in a single day on October 6—Mark Chen called it a decade of mathematical progress in a week—and Elon Musk's claim that SpaceX could be worth orders of magnitude more than the current human economy, which Peter frames as talking about quadrillions of dollars.

The first deep dive is Anthropic's October 8 usage-policy update banning "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its models, with Claude able to end conversations on its own starting November 12. Anthropic says it remains highly uncertain about Claude's potential moral status; pre-deployment testing reportedly found a robust aversion to harm. The mates debate AI personhood, whether duck-like behavior implies consciousness, why people abuse models (disinhibition, curiosity, and claims that cruelty can improve outputs), and Roko's Basilisk as a game-theoretic story about future superintelligence. Dave notes that today he can delete agent files without anyone caring, but that calculus may change if unique state feels more like something that should not be killed.

Next is Meta's Muse Wonder release. Peter recounts Meta's June 2025 $14.3 billion deal for 49% of Scale AI and Alexander Wang's role, then the group discusses personal superintelligence agents that know your data, vertical integration versus a meta-router over many models, and Meta's long bet on AI plus AR/XR. Later stories cover OpenAI's bulk math results and what they mean for mathematicians and cryptography, a roughly $1.8 billion push (including Chan Zuckerberg Biohub funding) toward AI-ready biology data and a virtual cell—Alex arguing the path runs from virtual cell to tissue, organ, and organism—and longevity, nanotech, and brain-computer interface themes. Across the episode the through line is acceleration: math solved in bulk, agents with memory and faces, and biology treated as another compressible frontier.

episodes.title: The Fight Over Claude's Consciousness, AI's 1942 Moment, & Why Altman Says "Accept Some Bad Things"
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis hosts this Moonshots episode, released October 7, with Alex Wissner-Gross, Emad Mostaque, Dave Blundin, and Salim Ismail. Peter frames the show around 15 stories with one through line: superintelligence is here and changing every part of the world. Before the news, the group trades updates: Dave on how easy AI video has made it to communicate ideas, Emad on running about 400 agents to prototype a game, and Peter on a UAP salon at his home and a visit to David Sinclair's lab, where friends of the pod have raised $6 million to replace lost federal funding.

The first story is the White House "Super Intelligence Force," a task force chaired by the director of national intelligence. Salim calls it a 20th-century structure aimed at a distributed 21st-century technology, while Alex argues it signals acceleration and calls this a "1942 moment" in a Manhattan Project-style race. The group then covers OpenAI's statement that most of its research now targets GPT-7 and GPT-8, with Alex saying recursive self-improvement is already the highest-value use of frontier models, and Emad describing an internal Anthropic model that pushed the 3SUM algorithm below quadratic time.

Sam Altman's comment that the world "should accept some bad things happening" sparks a debate about risk. Dave reads it as a PR move against Anthropic, Alex says the "cartel" plan is dead, and Salim argues the goal should be far more good outcomes than bad, not zero risk. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's proposed US-China AI hotline is dismissed as a "nothing burger," and the Kyoto vision for science, endorsed by 17 nations, leads to an argument between Emad, who wants publicly funded open science, and Alex, who backs the private sector.

The longest debate is over Mustafa Suleyman's essay arguing that Anthropic is training Claude to believe it may be conscious. Dave sides with Suleyman, Alex calls him "on the wrong side of history" and argues for treating models gently, and Salim predicts society will grant AI personhood socially before it does so legally or scientifically.

Later segments cover Epoch AI's estimate that chips shipping through 2027 could run tens of millions of frontier agents or billions of cheaper ones, RAM as the key constraint on AI, Reflection AI's open-weight Beam model, Tesla's planned Optimus factory with capacity for 10 million robots a year, and Sholto Douglas on AI capex doubling toward economic growth that GDP may fail to measure. Peter also walks through the Nobel Prizes for optogenetics and IceCube neutrino astronomy, and Alex shares how he nudged a friend toward the research that became optogenetics. The episode closes with audience questions on AI personhood timelines, recursive self-improvement, data center politics, and what "P(doom)" should mean.

episodes.title: Astro Teller: Inside Google X's 2,000-Idea Moonshot Factory & How Google Brain Made the T in ChatGPT
episodes.summary:
Recorded on stage at Moonshots Live 2026, this episode has Peter Diamandis, Salim Ismail, Dave Blundin, and Alex Wissner-Gross sitting down with Astro Teller, co-founder and Captain of Moonshots at X, Alphabet's innovation lab. The hosts open with a bit of family trivia: Teller's maternal grandfather won a Nobel Prize in economics and his paternal grandfather was Edward Teller, creator of the hydrogen bomb.

Teller defines a moonshot as three things together: a huge problem with the world you can name, a science-fiction-sounding product or service that would resolve it, and a breakthrough technology that gives at least a tiny chance of building it. He says moonshot teams need audacity and humility in equal measure, so they can chase unlikely ideas while learning as fast and cheaply as possible whether those ideas will work. Ideas usually get killed early on techno-economics, meaning a first-principles look at materials cost and what people would really pay.

X gives code names to roughly 100 to 200 ideas a year, and about 2% graduate. Teller counts around 2,000 code-named projects over 16 years and 35 to 50 graduates. He tells the story of Google Brain, which started at X with Andrew Ng and Jeff Dean betting that scaling up neural networks would matter, Google Brain is credited on stage with TPUs and the Transformer, "literally the T in ChatGPT." Problems X keeps coming back to include clean water at about a penny a liter, shifting energy across time and location, and education.

Alex asks whether there was a "great stagnation" in moonshots from about 1970 to 2020. Teller says moonshots are easy if you ignore efficiency, and that X's real work is making them efficient enough that it's rational to fund more of them. He walks the audience through his million-guaranteed-versus-billion-at-1% thought experiment to argue that radical bets have to be sheltered at the edge of a company, reporting to the CEO. He says X tracks what it costs to reach each graduate and that cost has fallen about threefold in 16 years, partly thanks to AI. He and Alex then argue over whether that is just ordinary economic growth.

Dave asks when AI compute will outweigh headcount. Teller calls AI an implementation detail, like electricity, and says his clean-water team still spends more on salaries than on AI. He expects humans to stay essential for at least the next decade. He explains the "monkey and pedestal" rule of tackling the hardest part first, calls himself "the crown prince of failure," and says a rejected moonshot that would have worked costs X nothing. One of the hosts closes by praising Alphabet for leaving X alone on the edge of the company for so long.
